market_holds: Front-week options (sealed 18:11 UTC, expiry 11-13) price a 15.0% straddle, about 8.55% for the event once ordinary vol is netted out. Skew is -4.15 vol points, so the market pays more for calls than puts, and put/call OI is 0.48. The price holds a violent re-rating on the AST SpaceMobile deal. The stock closed at a 52-week low of 15.18 on Nov 5, then made 20.76 on Nov 6 (deal announced, +36.8%) and 24.31 on Nov 9 (+17.1%, the day AST's 10-Q disclosed $400m cash plus 10-14m AST shares for the licence). It traded around 23.3 intraday today, about -4%, even with a Synspective launch deal announced today. That is +53% in three sessions (Yahoo daily bars). Q3 consensus is about $104-106m revenue and an EPS loss of about -$0.49 to -$0.52. The Earnings Whispers preview is dated Nov 3, so it predates the deal. Q4 consensus is about $137m, putting FY at about $440m, the upper half of the $420-450m guide reiterated on Aug 11 (company release). KeyBanc cut its target from 50 to 35 on Nov 2, and no post-deal estimate revisions were found. The last four reactions were small or mixed: +0.7% (Aug 11, a 34% revenue beat that was offset by the Alpha slip), -5.5%, +1.1%, and +17.0% in Nov 2025.
view: This print is no longer a quarter. It is the first time Firefly management explains the AST engine and licence deal (the Nov 6 release says it will be discussed on this call), and it lands after a +53% three-session squeeze off the 52-week low. The parts the market already has: the headline >$1.3bn; the split from AST's 10-Q filed Nov 9 ($400m cash plus 10-14m AST Class A shares for a perpetual licence, the rest for 36 engines and 3 years of engineering support); and the fact that the deal is still a 'proposed transaction' that has not closed. The parts it does not have, and that the release or call will reveal: (1) when it closes and when the cash arrives; (2) how Firefly will recognise the licence, either at a point in time (which could swell 2026 or 2027 GAAP revenue and the guide by hundreds of millions) or over the three-year support period; (3) whether the $420-450m 2026 guide survives. That guide depends on a Q4 near $135m, and Alpha Flight 8, promised for Q4, shows no public trace of acceptance testing, shipment to Vandenberg or a static fire since the Aug 11 slip. The company's news page lists no Alpha flight item since August, only new contracts (CLPS 2 vendor Nov 7, Synspective up to 10 Alphas Nov 10). Blue Ghost Mission 2 is still officially '2026', and one tracker shows a NET 2027 placeholder. So the print has a credible upside path (fast close, point-in-time licence revenue, a raised or reframed outlook, cash that removes the burn worry) and a credible downside path (Alpha slips to 2027, the guide narrows to the low end, a cost-to-cost margin hit, details that are mostly stock with lock-ups, and sell-the-news after a 53% squeeze). The two paths are roughly balanced and I cannot weight either side from public evidence. The options already price a large move with an upside lean. I see the size, not the direction.

recommendation.reason: The decisive item is the accounting and timing of the AST licence, and it is unknown on both sides. The Q3 quarter itself has been a weak driver of the stock (+0.7% on a 34% revenue beat in August). The likely Alpha Flight 8 slip is real but small in revenue terms, and after a 53% squeeze it could just as easily be shrugged off as punished. Nothing I found shows a gap between the price and the release in one direction.
recommendation.what_would_flip_it: A statement in the release that the licence closes in Q4 2026 with the $400m cash and point-in-time revenue recognition (a raised 2026 outlook) would make me lean long. A guide cut below $420m, or Alpha Flight 8 moved to 2027 with no AST closing date, would make me lean short.

questions_pursued.question: What are the AST deal's economics, and are they already public?
questions_pursued.how: Firefly release (finviz), EDGAR full-text search for AST filings, AST 10-Q Note 15
questions_pursued.answer: Firefly gave no split. AST's 10-Q (Nov 9) gave $400m cash plus 10-14m shares for the licence, with lock-ups, and said the deal has not closed. The stock rose 17% that day.
questions_pursued.moved_view: The deal split is largely priced. What remains is closing timing and Firefly's revenue recognition, which is unknown in direction. It kept p_up at 50.

self_critique: Long case: a 53% squeeze driven by a deal management will now explain, call skew already leaning up, and a company feeding good news into the print (CLPS 2, Synspective). If the licence is recognised at closing in Q4, the guide headline could more than double and algorithms would chase it. Short case: a three-session +53% move off a 52-week low into a print where the core business likely shows a Q4 Alpha slip and a guide at the low end is a classic sell-the-news setup. Today's -4% on a positive contract headline hints that supply is coming in. Both are plausible; neither has evidence that dominates.
approach_notes: The P3 'stakeholder filings' route paid off: the counterparty's 10-Q held the deal terms the company had not given. The P4 'priced in is a claim to prove' test helped separate what was already public (the split) from what was not (accounting, closing). Nothing in the playbook helps weight a binary accounting disclosure that has no public lead.
